Ms Kemmy Tan was appointed executive director and chief executive officer (CEO) of 
the manager on 1 July 2026, succeeding the former CEO who had been in the role for more 
than 16 years.  
 
The profile of the executive director and CEO is set out on pages 19 and 22 of the annual 
report.  
 
(i) 
What were the key criteria used by the board when selecting a new CEO? In 
particular, how did the board assess the importance of retail industry 
experience, 
investment 
and 
asset-management 
track 
record, 
understanding of REITs, capital allocation capabilities and other skills that 
it considers critical to leading the manager and repositioning the REIT for 
its next phase of growth? 
 
No performance fee was earned by the manager for the year ended 30 June 2026, as the 
performance of the Trust Index was approximately 75% below the benchmark index as at 
30 June 2026. As at 30 June 2015, the underperformance was approximately 1%. This 
represents a significant deterioration in relative performance over the past decade.  
 
(ii) 
What are the three most important changes that the new CEO intends to 
make to the REIT’s strategy or operating model, based on her assessment of 
the factors behind the REIT’s past performance? 
 
(iii) 
Given the REIT’s current size, discount to NAV and acquisition capacity, what 
are the realistic avenues for growth? Which growth opportunities or 
strategic initiatives will be priorities for the new CEO?

Excluding the impact of the divestment of the Wisma Atria office strata units, the 
portfolio valuation would have increased by 0.2% year-on-year. However, the reported fair 
value movements across the portfolio were significantly affected by foreign exchange 
movements. In particular, the Australia Properties1 increased in Singapore dollar terms by 
S$4.2 million despite a decline in Australian dollar terms (down A$21.2 million) and the 
Malaysia Properties showed a significant positive change (5.1% or S$21.3 million) despite a 
RM1 million valuation decline.  
 
 
1 The combined valuation of the Australia Properties was S$336.1 million (A$377.5 million) as at 30 June 
2026, increasing by S$4.2 million from a year ago mainly due to the appreciation of the Australian dollar 
against Singapore dollar. In Australian dollar terms, the valuation declined by A$21.2 million across both 
Adelaide and Perth properties, primarily due to lower income assumptions for Myer Centre Adelaide 
following the unmaterialised activation of Level 5 and softer market rent assumptions. 

(Source: annual report) 
 
(i) 
Foreign exchange effects: Would the board consider providing property 
valuations and year-on-year valuation movements of each property in both 
Singapore dollar and local currency terms in future annual reports and 
presentations? This would allow unitholders to distinguish changes in 
underlying property value from movements arising from foreign exchange. 
 
(ii) 
Myer Centre Adelaide: Myer currently occupies approximately 324,000 square 
feet in the property. Following the arbitration in which Myer’s claim for a 
declaration that it was entitled to terminate its lease was dismissed, what is 
the current working relationship between the manager and Myer? Given 
that the lease expires in 2032 and Myer contributed approximately 7.7% of 
the REIT’s total revenue as at 30 June 2026, what is the board’s assessment 
of the key risks to the income stream over the remaining lease term, and

(iii) 
Markor: A new tenant, 成都二十四城装饰工程有限公司,commenced its lease in

Markor ceased making rental payments, the total rental arrears

Revenue from the China Property was reported to be $1.5 million in FY2026, 
compared with $1.6 million in each of FY2025 and FY2024. To what extent did 
the reported rental income in these years translate into cash collections, 

and how much remained uncollected from Markor? Of the $1.45 million

will the manager use to assess whether the new tenancy has stabilised the

China: The carrying value of the China Property2 has fallen to $9.5 million, from

on what basis did the audit committee satisfy itself that the $22.2 million 
valuation was reasonable and supportable?

qa.question:
Despite a 24% increase in revenue in FY2026, profit before tax fell 57% to $13.3 million 
as gross profit decreased from $80.2 million to $68.7 million, largely due to lower margins 
in the cable and wire (C&W) segment, after the provision for onerous contracts.  
(Source: company annual report) 
 
While C&W segment revenue increased by 11.9%, from $343.3 million to $384.1 million, 
segment results fell sharply from $28.5 million to just $7.0 million, reflecting the impact of 
provisions for onerous contracts. 
 
As highlighted in the key audit matter 1 (KAM), the group enters into fixed-price sales 
contracts for cable deliveries. Its gross margins are exposed to fluctuations in copper prices 
because manufacturing costs can rise while contracted selling prices remain unchanged. As 
at 30 June 2026, prevailing copper prices exceeded the fixed selling prices under certain 
contracts with deliveries scheduled over the following one to three and a half years. The 
group consequently recognised an onerous contract provision of $23.89 million, compared 
with $0.76 million in FY2025. 
 
(i) 
Given the volatility of copper prices and delivery periods of up to three and 
a half years, what commercial rationale supported accepting these fixed-
price contracts, and what protections were in place against rising input 
costs? At the point of contract award, what minimum gross margins and 
 
1 The “provision for onerous contracts” is a key audit matter highlighted by the independent auditor. Key 
audit matters are those matters that, in the professional judgement of the independent auditor, were of most 
significance in the audit of the financial statements of the current period. 

copper-price assumptions were used to assess profitability, and how did 
these assumptions compare with actual outcomes? 
 
(ii) 
Has management considered incorporating copper-price pass-through 
clauses, shorter pricing validity periods or other contractual safeguards 
into orders? If these protections are not commercially feasible, how does the 
group price the commodity price risk?  
 
(iii) 
What specific hedging strategy does the group use to manage copper-price 
exposure arising from committed sales orders, and to what extent did this 
strategy mitigate the impact of copper-price movements in FY2026? What 
explains the substantial increase in onerous contract provisions despite the 
use of copper derivatives, and what oversight does the board exercise over 
these exposures and the effectiveness of the hedging strategy? 
 
Furthermore, in Note 10 (Derivative financial instruments; page 130), the company 
disclosed the following:  
 
As at 30 June 2026 and 30 June 2025, the group and the company had outstanding 
copper contracts that were used to hedge significant future fluctuations in copper 
prices. The fair value liabilities of copper contracts for the group was [sic] $976,000 (30 
June 2025: fair value assets of $283,000). The company had no outstanding copper 
contracts as at 30 June 2026 (30 June 2025: fair value asset of $340,000)… 
 
(iv) 
Given that the group’s copper derivatives had a net fair value liability of 
$976,000 as at 30 June 2026, does this indicate that the group held net short 
positions in copper or did it enter into the contract when copper hit a high? 
What underlying exposure were these positions intended to hedge, and how 
did management determine the appropriate direction and size of the 
contracts? 
 
(v) 
What control does the board have in place to ensure that copper derivatives 
are used solely to hedge identifiable business exposures and are not 
speculative in nature?

the acquisition2 of solar distribution businesses in Thailand and the Philippines, with the aim 
of capturing growing demand for renewable energy.

terminating the compressed natural gas purchase agreement. The termination arose from 
the customer’s decision to transition its operational energy and fuelling requirements from 
CNG to liquefied natural gas (LNG).  
 
Consequently, the group's CNG supply business and related products and services were 
terminated in May 2026. 
 
Management has stated that it remains focused on its remaining core businesses. 
 
(i) 
Can management clarify whether, under the terms of the purchase 
agreement, any compensation was received from the customer? Was the 
risk of the customer transitioning away from CNG identified during the risk 
assessments by the board/management, and what contingency plans had 
been developed? Within what timeframe does the board expect the group to 
recover the revenue lost from the discontinued CNG business? 
 
(ii) 
Prior to the customer’s termination, did the board assess the long-term 
commercial viability of the CNG business as customers transition towards 
alternative fuels? Specifically, did the group evaluate whether its existing 
capabilities, customer relationships and infrastructure could be adapted to 
serve the LNG market or other energy solutions? What commercial and 
investment criteria led the board to pursue or reject these alternatives? 
 
(iii) 
Has the group downsized the workforce, including making appropriate 
adjustments to the responsibilities and remuneration of senior 
management following the loss of this core business?

The group's financial highlights in the annual report (page 11) indicate that natural gas-
related businesses accounted for more than 75% of total revenue. 

(Source: company annual report; emphasis added)  
 
(i) 
Could the board clarify the nature and scale of the group's remaining 
businesses, particularly its manufacturing and trading activities involving 
cleanroom-grade plastic packaging bags and materials used to package 
finished products for hard disk drive and semiconductor customers? Is the 
manufacturing facility located in Malaysia, and are its customers primarily 
based in Thailand? What are the business's key sources of competitive 
advantage, and how does the group differentiate itself from competing 
suppliers in terms of product quality, technical capabilities, cost, reliability 
or customer relationships? 
 
(ii) 
To what extent has the group been able to capture the growth in the 
semiconductor industry, driven by an investment boom in data centres and 
AI infrastructure?  
 
As at 30 June 2026, the company has accumulated losses of $(45.5) million and total equity 
of just $1.68 million, against share capital of $48.6 million. After 27 years as a listed company, 

the group's revenue remains in the low single-digit millions, and it recently lost a major 
customer. The market capitalisation1 of the company is approximately $8 million.  
 
(iii) 
What is the board's concrete plan to achieve sustainable growth? Given the 
company’s long history as a listed company, the current limited scale, and 
weak capital position, what evidence supports the board's confidence that 
its remaining or new businesses can achieve meaningful growth and 
generate acceptable returns for minority shareholders? What specific 
milestones has the board set for management over the next three years, and 
how will it hold management accountable for meeting them?

The company announced on 3 July 2026 that its subsidiary, Leverage Income Sdn. Bhd., 
had entered into a sale and purchase agreement with an independent third party to sell five 
three-storey shop offices in Penang, Malaysia, for MYR20.5 million (approximately S$6.5 
million).  
 
The sale was completed on 22 September 2026. 
 
(i) 
What has been the total shareholder return over the past 5, 10, 15, 20 and 
27 years since its listing on SESDAQ in September 1999? 
 
(ii) 
In light of the company's long-term shareholder returns and the recent 
disposal proceeds of approximately S$6.5 million, has the board considered 
a capital reduction or other form of capital return to shareholders? What 
constraints or competing capital requirements would justify retaining the 
proceeds rather than allowing shareholders to allocate the capital 
themselves?

qa.question:
Would the board and management provide unitholders with greater clarity on the 
following operational and financial matters? Specifically: 
 
(i) 
PLQ Mall: Has the mall performed up to management’s expectations since 
the acquisition, and what return does management expect to generate from 
the reconfiguration of approximately 16,000 sq ft of retail space?  
 
(ii) 
Milan: While Buildings 1 and 2 are fully leased to Sky Italia through January 2033, 
Building 3 has been configured for multi-tenancy with a committed occupancy of 
approximately 51%. What was the average actual occupancy of Building 3 
during FY2026? Does the manager expect to market all three buildings as a 
portfolio, or would it consider divesting Buildings 1 and 2 separately given 
their long-term lease to Sky Italia? 
 
(iii) 
Grange House: The 3,000-capacity purpose-built entertainment venue next to 
313@somerset is expected to be operationally ready in mid-2027. Can 
management elaborate on the business and revenue model of the venue? 
 
(iv) 
Rental reversion and tenant retention rate: Has the manager benchmarked 
the 11.7% rental reversion for retail and tenant retention rate of 70.8% 
over an extended leasing cycle?

As at 30 June 2026, the REIT’s gross borrowings stood at $1.71 billion, with aggregate 
leverage ratio at 38.9%. While the interest coverage ratio improved from 1.6 times to 2.1 
times, it remains relatively low. The REIT reported a weighted average cost of debt of 2.75% 
per annum, down from 3.46% a year ago.   
 
(i) 
Weighted average cost of debt: The reported average cost of debt excludes 
amortisation of debt-related transaction costs (and other fees). What is the all-
in weighted average cost of debt? When evaluating refinancing, new debt or 
other funding options, does the manager assess funding costs on an all-in 
basis, including transaction costs, fees and other financing-related 
expenses? 
 
(ii) 
Perpetual securities: The REIT redeemed $200 million of Perpetual Securities 
Series 001, which carried a coupon of 4.20%, while issuing $120 million of new 
Perpetual Securities Series 004 at a higher coupon rate of 4.28%. Can the board 
explain the role of perpetual securities within the REIT's overall capital 
management strategy? In particular, how does the manager assess the 
economic cost of perpetual securities against bank borrowings? To what 
extent did the manager choose to issue the Series 004 perpetual securities 
and not to take up additional bank borrowings so as to maintain the REIT’s 
aggregate leverage?

At the close of the REIT’s preferential offering on 18 March 2026, valid acceptances 
amounted to 53.05% of the units available for subscription, with a further 9.14% of units 
taken up through excess applications. 
 
(Source: 
https://links.sgx.com/FileOpen/Results%20of%20Preferential%20Offering_Final.ashx?Ap
p=Announcement&FileID=880048) 
 
(i) 
Has the manager undertaken a post-mortem analysis of the preferential 
offering to understand the low level of valid acceptances? In particular, 
what did the manager learn from the take-up to indicate about unitholders' 
willingness to commit additional capital to the REIT, and did the manager 
identify any concerns relating to the terms of the offering, pricing, 
underlying asset or the track record of the manager? 
 
(ii) 
How did the manager come to believe that a non-renounceable preferential 
offering was the most appropriate method of raising capital in the 
circumstances? How did the independent directors assess the impact on 
unitholders who were unwilling or unable to commit additional capital? 
Also, how did the independent directors satisfy themselves that the terms 
and structure of the preferential offering appropriately balanced the REIT's 
funding requirements with the interests of existing unitholders? 
 
Separately, the REIT also conducted a private placement in November 2025 in which new 
units were issued at $0.602 per unit, compared with the last reported net asset value per 
unit of $0.75, representing a discount of 20%. The private placement raised gross proceeds 
of no less than $270 million to support the acquisition of PLQ Mall. 
 
(iii) 
Can the independent directors provide unitholders with justification why 
placing out new units at a 20% discount to acquire an asset at 2.2% discount 
to its appraised value is in the interest of minority unitholders?

accounting profit, net cash outflow from operating activities amounted to $(2.31) million,

to 80 days.

conversion and align operating cash flow more closely with reported

two years.

https://www.sgxgroup.com/media-centre/20260116-regulators-column-forward-

(i) 
Given SGX RegCo’s encouragement of forward guidance and its view that

board considered providing forward guidance for FY26/27 on the group’s 
performance, outlook, key operating assumptions, and strategic priorities? 
If not, why not?
